draft.title: The Ottawa Charter
card: The Ottawa Charter is a framework for health promotion released by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 1986. It lists five action areas that governments, services and communities can use.

laws and rules that make healthy choices easier, such as tobacco taxes or helmet laws. Supportive environments: safe, healthy places to live, learn and work, such as shaded playgrounds or smoke-free venues.
local groups set their own health goals and work together to reach them. Personal skills: teaching people knowledge and skills, such as how to cook, manage stress or read food labels.
shifting services from treating illness only to also preventing it and keeping people well, such as a clinic that runs screening and health education.
draft.remember: The five action areas are policy, environments, community action, personal skills and health services.

a.q: A council bans smoking in all outdoor dining areas. Which Ottawa Charter action area is this?
a.why: A ban is a rule made by a council, so it is healthy public policy. It is not developing personal skills, because it changes the rules and does not teach people anything new.
a.clue: Think about who made the rule.

b.q: A clinic in Wagga Wagga adds free sessions on healthy eating and quitting smoking, so it helps people stay well and not only treats illness. Which action area does this best show?
b.why: The clinic is changing what a health service does, from treating illness to also keeping people well. Developing personal skills is tempting because the sessions teach people, but the main change here is to the service itself.
b.clue: Focus on what changed about the clinic.

problems.detail: The stem says the clinic now 'helps people stay well and not only treats illness'. This nearly repeats the card's definition of reorienting health services, so a student can match the words without knowing the idea.

proposal.title: The Ottawa Charter
card: The Ottawa Charter is a framework for health promotion released by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 1986. It sets out five action areas that governments, services and communities can use.

Building healthy public policy: laws and rules that make healthy choices easier, such as tobacco taxes or helmet laws. Creating supportive environments: safe, healthy places to live, learn and work, such as shaded playgrounds or well-lit bike paths.

Strengthening community action: local groups set their own health goals and work together to reach them. Developing personal skills: teaching people knowledge and skills, such as how to cook or read food labels.
Reorienting health services: shifting health services from only treating illness to also preventing it, such as a clinic that adds screening tests.
proposal.remember: Five action areas: public policy, supportive environments, community action, personal skills and reorienting health services.

a.why: A ban is a rule made by a council, so it is healthy public policy. It is not developing personal skills, because it changes the rules and does not teach people anything new.
a.clue: Think about who made the rule.

b.q: A hospital in Wagga Wagga moves some nurses from its wards to run free blood pressure checks at local shopping centres. Which action area is this?
b.why: The hospital is changing how its own staff work, moving from caring for sick patients toward finding problems early. That is reorienting health services. It is not creating supportive environments, because the shopping centre itself is not made any safer or healthier.
b.clue: Whose work has changed, and toward what?
